question: Which of the following books was written by the Roman writer Pliny the elder?
solution:
The correct answer is __Natural History.__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**

__
 
• Natural History__ was written by the __Roman writer Pliny__ the Elder in __77 AD__, who wrote in this book that __Rome__ was wasting its gold reserves by trading with India.

 __
 
• Pliny the Elder wrote a book titled "The Natural History", often known as Naturalis Historia.
 
• Natural History gathers data from various ancient authors and is the largest single work to have survived from the Roman Empire to the present.
 
• Despite the work's title, Pliny himself characterizes his subject matter as "the natural world, or life," rather than what is currently recognized as natural history.
 
• Its scope is encyclopedic, although its organization differs from that of a contemporary encyclopedia.
 
• It was Pliny's final publication and the only one of his writings to have survived. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information:__**

 
• Periplus of the Erythraean Sea:

 
 
• ​The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, also known by its Latin name, the Periplus Maris Erythraei, is a Greco-Roman periplus that describes trade and navigation opportunities from Roman Egyptian ports along the Red Sea coast, such as Berenice Troglodytica, as well as those along the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean, including the modern-day Sindh region of Pakistan and the southwest of India.
 
 
 
• Indica:
 
 
• ​The Greek author Megasthenes' account of Mauryan India is titled Indika.
 
• Although the original work is now lost, succeeding Greek and Latin writings still have some of its parts.
 
 
 
• Geographica:
 
 
• ​The Geographica, or Geography, is a collection of 17 Greek-language "books" that serves as an encyclopaedia of geographic information.
 
• It is credited to Strabo, a learned Roman citizen of Greek heritage.

question: India was named ‘Bharat’ after the name of the Bharat tribe. In which of the following Vedas is this tribe first mentioned?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rigveda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** Bharatas were the Vedic tribe mentioned in Rigveda. The name Bharata was used for a group of people who lived in the northwest, and who are mentioned in the Rigveda, the earliest composition in Sanskrit. Later it was used for the country.

__
 
• Vedic Period__

 __
 
• It is the period in the late Bronze age and early Iron Age of the History of India when the Vedas were composed in the northern Indian subcontinent.
 
• The associated culture was referred to as Vedic Civilization.
 
• The entire Earth was called the Bharatvarsha but in particular, the area that lied south to the Himalayan Mountain was called the Bharatvarsha.
 
• The Bharatvarsha was also known as Aryavarta meaning the land of Aryans.
 
• Aryavarta and Bharat are mentioned in Vedas, many scriptures, and Mahabharata.
 
• Bharatas were the Vedic tribe mentioned in Rigveda.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Rig Veda: 

 
 
• The **oldest Veda** is the Rigveda.
 
• It has **1028 hymns** called ‘**Suktas’** and is a collection of 10 books called **Mandalas**.
 
• The meaning of the word ‘Rigveda’ is **Praise Knowledge**. 
 
• Rigvedic books 2-9 deal with cosmology and deities.
 
• Rigvedic books 1 and 10 deal with philosophical questions and also talk about various virtues including charity in society. 
 
• The meters used to form hymns are Gayatri, Anushtubh, Trishtubh, and Jagati (**Trishtubh and Gayatri are most important**).
 
 
 
• Sama Veda:
 
 
• Known as the Veda of** melodies **and** chants**, Samaveda dates back to **1200-800 BCE**.
 
• This Veda is related to public worship. T
 
• here are **1549 verses **(except 75 verses, all have been taken from Rigveda). 
 
• There are two Upanishads embedded in Samaveda – **Chandogya Upanishad** and **Kena Upanishad**.
 
• Samaveda Samhita is not meant to be read as a text, it is like a musical score sheet that must be heard. 
 
 
 
• ​Yajur Veda:
 
 
• Stands to mean ‘**Worship Knowledge**’.
 
• Yajurveda dates back to **1100-800 BCE**.
 
• It compiles ritual-offering mantras/chants. These chants were offered by the priest alongside a person who used to perform a ritual (in most cases yajna fire.)
 
• It has two types –** Krishna **(Black/Dark) & Shukla (White/Bright). Krishna Yajurveda has an un-arranged, unclear, motley collection of verses and Shukla Yajurveda has arranged and clear verses.
 
 
 
• ​Atharva Veda:
 
 
• Stands to mean a tatpurusha compound of Atharvan, an ancient sage, and knowledge.
 
• It dates back to** 1000-800 BCE**.
 
• It has **730 hymns/suktas,** **6000** mantras, and **20 books**.

question: According to which of the following foreign travellers did Dhruvasena II attend Harsha’s assembly at Prayag (Allahabad)?
solution:
The correct answer is **Hiuen Tsang**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hiuen Tsang**, also known as Xuanzang, was a Chinese Buddhist monk, scholar, traveller, and translator who visited India during the reign of King Harshavardhana.
 
• He came to India in the 7th century (precisely around 630 AD) to acquire Buddhist texts and to study at the ancient university of Nalanda.
 
• Hiuen Tsang's detailed accounts provide valuable insights into the political, social, and religious life of India during this period.
 
• He attended the assembly at Prayag (Allahabad) organized by King Harsha, which was a significant religious gathering attended by scholars, monks, and dignitaries from different parts.
 
• His works, especially the **Si-Yu-Ki** or the **Records of the Western World**, are crucial sources of historical information not only about India but also about other regions in Central Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
 

 Aspect
 Description
 
 
 
 

 **Prayag Assembly**
 Organized by King Harsha, it was a grand religious gathering that attracted scholars, monks, and dignitaries, showcasing the religious tolerance and patronage of Buddhism.
 
 

 **Nalanda University**
 An ancient center of higher learning in Bihar, India, famous for its Buddhist scholarship but also taught other subjects.
 
 

 **Buddhist Pilgrimage**
 Hiuen Tsang's journey to India was part of a broader tradition of Buddhist monks travelling to gain knowledge and religious texts.
 
 

 **Translation Work**
 After returning to China, Hiuen Tsang dedicated his life to translating the Buddhist scriptures he had collected into Chinese, significantly influencing Chinese Buddhism.
 
 

 **Legacy**
 Hiuen Tsang is remembered for his contributions to the spread of Buddhism and for his detailed accounts that offer insights into medieval Indian history.

question: Pushyamitra, who was the commander of Brihadratha, the last Mauryan emperor, killed the king and established a new dynasty. Which of the following was his dynasty?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Option 1**__. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** Pushyamitra**, the commander of **Brihadratha**, established the **Shunga dynasty** after killing the** last Mauryan emperor**.
 
• **The Shunga dynasty **ruled over** North India** from around **185 BCE to 73 BCE.**
 
• **Pushyamitra** is said to have been a **Brahmin** and a follower of Brahmanism, which may have played a role in his overthrow of the **Mauryan dynasty, which was associated with Buddhism.​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Kanva dynasty** was a **short-lived dynasty** that ruled over the** Magadha region** of ancient India from around **73 BCE to 28 BCE**.

 
 
• It was founded by** Vasudeva, **a minister of the last **Shunga emperor,** who took advantage of a power vacuum to establish himself as the **ruler of Magadha.** The Kanva dynasty is considered to be a minor dynasty in Indian history, and little is known about its rulers and their accomplishments.
 
• The most notable ruler of the **Kanva dynasty** was probably** Bhumimitra**, who is known for his inscriptions and for his patronage of Buddhism.
 
• The** Kanva dynasty** was eventually overthrown by the **Satavahanas**, a dynasty from the Deccan region of India.
 
 
 
• **The Satavahana dynasty **was a prominent **ancient Indian dynasty** that ruled over a large part of South and Central India.
 
 
• The Satavahanas were known for their patronage of** Buddhism and Hinduism,** and their rule is considered to be a period of great cultural and economic prosperity in the region.
 
• During their rule, the Satavahanas issued a large number of** inscriptions, coins, and other artifacts, which have provided valuable insights into their culture, religion, and social and economic life.**
 
• They were also known for their contributions to **architecture, literature, and art,** including the creation of the famous** Buddhist stupa at Amaravati.**
 
 
 
• **​The Chedi dynasty** was an ancient Indian dynasty that ruled in the region of present-day** Bundelkhand in central India**.
 
 
• The dynasty is believed to have been founded by **Shishupala**, who was a cousin of **Lord Krishna**.
 
• The Chedi dynasty is mentioned in various** ancient Hindu texts, including the Mahabharata and the Puranas.**
 
• The dynasty is said to have been one of the most powerful in ancient India and is believed to have flourished between the **6th century BCE and the 5th century CE.**

question: Mathura was the second capital of _________ dynasty.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Kushana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Kushana dynasty was a prominent dynasty in ancient India, known for its significant role in the development of culture and trade.
 
• Mathura served as the second capital of the Kushana dynasty, with the first capital being Purushapura (modern-day Peshawar).
 
• Kanishka, one of the most notable rulers of the Kushana dynasty, played a crucial role in promoting Buddhism and patronizing art and culture.
 
• The Kushanas are well-known for their contributions to the spread of Mahayana Buddhism across the Indian subcontinent and Central Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kanishka the Great:**

 
 
• Kanishka was a renowned emperor of the Kushana dynasty, ruling during the 2nd century CE.
 
• He is credited with organizing the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, which led to the formal adoption of Mahayana Buddhism.
 
• Kanishka is also known for his patronage of art, architecture, and the establishment of the Silk Road.
 
 
 
• **Kushana Coinage:**
 
 
• The Kushanas introduced gold coinage in India, which featured the images of their kings and various deities.
 
• Their coins played a significant role in facilitating trade and commerce in the region.
 
 
 
• **Gandhara Art:**
 
 
• The Kushana period saw the flourishing of Gandhara art, which is a unique blend of Indian and Greco-Roman artistic traditions.
 
• This style is particularly noted for its exquisite Buddhist sculptures and stupas.
 
 
 
• **Silk Road:**
 
 
• The Kushanas played a pivotal role in the development of the Silk Road, which was a network of trade routes connecting the East and West.
 
• This facilitated cultural exchanges and the spread of Buddhism across Asia.

• that spans the prehistoric Paleolithic and Mesolithic periods, as well as the historic period.

question: Which historical process is best reflected by the evolution of temple architecture in India?

options.text: Continuous interaction of religion and regional styles

solution:
The correct answer is __**Continuous interaction of religion and regional styles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The evolution of temple architecture in India reflects the **continuous interaction of religion and regional styles**. Temples were designed to serve as physical representations of religious ideologies and as centers of socio-cultural activities.
 
• India's temple architecture developed over centuries, influenced by various religious beliefs like **Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism**, and shaped by local cultural elements like art, geography, and climate.
 
• **Regional variations:** Northern India saw the rise of the Nagara style, characterized by curved towers (Shikharas), while South India developed the Dravida style, marked by pyramid-shaped towers (Vimanas). The Vesara style emerged as a blend of these two in central India.
 
• Each dynasty and region added its unique touch to temple architecture, such as the intricacy of **Chola temples in Tamil Nadu**, the grandeur of **Kalinga temples in Odisha**, and the symmetry of **Khajuraho temples in Madhya Pradesh**.
 
• Religious ideologies were often intertwined with regional aesthetics, as seen in the carvings, sculptures, and ornamentation that depicted local deities, myths, and folklore.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Temple Architecture Styles in India:**

 
 
• **Nagara Style (North India):** Featured curved towers (Shikharas), smaller, sanctum-centric designs, and intricate carvings. Examples: **Sun Temple, Konark**; **Kandariya Mahadev, Khajuraho**.
 
• **Dravida Style (South India):** Characterized by pyramid-like Vimanas, gopurams (ornate gateways), and large temple complexes. Examples: **Brihadeeswarar Temple, Thanjavur**; **Meenakshi Temple, Madurai**.
 
• **Vesara Style (Deccan Region):** A fusion of Nagara and Dravida styles, often seen in Karnataka and Maharashtra. Example: **Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Religion:**
 
 
• Religious ideologies influenced temple rituals, which in turn dictated architectural designs, such as the sanctum's sacred geometry.
 
• Temples served as centers of learning, cultural activities, and community gatherings, reflecting their religious significance in society.
 
 
 
• **Important Dynasties and Contributions:**
 
 
• **Cholas:** Known for massive Dravida-style temples like the Brihadeeswarar Temple.
 
• **Pallavas:** Developed early Dravidian architecture; examples include the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram.
 
• **Guptas:** Pioneered Nagara-style temples, such as the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh.
 
• **Hoysalas:** Created elaborately sculpted Vesara-style temples like the Chennakesava Temple, Belur.
 
 
 
• **Features of Temple Architecture:**
 
 
• Elements like **Garbhagriha** (sanctum sanctorum), **Shikhara/Vimana** (tower), **Mandapa** (hall), and **Pradakshina Patha** (circumambulatory path).
 
• Intricate carvings depicting religious themes, mythology, and social life.
 
• Use of local materials like granite in Tamil Nadu and sandstone in Rajasthan.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sudden cultural change:** Incorrect. Temple architecture evolved gradually over centuries, shaped by regional and religious influences.
 
• **Foreign architectural dominance:** Incorrect. While some foreign elements were incorporated (like Mughal influence in Indo-Islamic architecture), temple architecture is predominantly indigenous.
 
• **Decline of indigenous art:** Incorrect. Temple architecture represents a flourishing of indigenous art, not its decline.
 
• **Continuous interaction of religion and regional styles:** Correct. Indian temple architecture is a product of the dynamic interplay between religious beliefs and local cultural aesthetics.

question:
With the 2022 amendments to the Indian Constitution, which of the following communities have been granted the Scheduled Tribes status by the Government of India?

A. Narikoravan community

B. Hattee community

C. Kadu Kuruba community

D. Kapu community
solution:
The correct answer is **A, B and C only** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**

 
• In 2022, the Lok Sabha received the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order (Second Amendment) Bill.
 
• Arjun Munda introduced it in the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950, as it relates to Tamil Nadu, is to be amended by the bill.
 
• In states and union territories, the Order identifies the tribal groups that are considered to be Scheduled Tribes.
 
• After this Bill is approved, the Gond group will be moved from the list of SCs to the list of STs, and the Dhuria, Nayak, Ojha, Pathari, and Rajgond will be added to the list of STs in Uttar Pradesh in the four districts of Sant Kabir Nagar, Kushinagar, Chandauli, and Bhadohi.
 
• The Narikoravan and Kurivikkaran communities are listed among the Scheduled Tribes in the Bill in Tamil Nadu.

 
• The **Bill will amend the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950**, for inclusion of the Hattee community of the **Trans Giri area of the Sirmour district of Himachal Pradesh in the list of Scheduled Tribes.**
 
• In the **Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950, in PART VI.**—Karnataka added **Kadu Kuruba, Betta-Kuruba.**

question: Dr. Bhupen Hazarika is famously known by which of the following titles, reflecting his deep connection to the geography and spirit of Assam?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bard of Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dr. Bhupen Hazarika** is one of India's most celebrated musicians, lyricists, and cultural icons. He is fondly referred to as the **"Bard of Brahmaputra"**, highlighting his deep connection to the Brahmaputra River and Assam's culture.
 
• The title “Bard of Brahmaputra” reflects his lifelong association with the **Brahmaputra River**, which is central to the life and culture of Assam. His songs and compositions often depicted the river’s significance in the lives of the Assamese people.
 
• Dr. Bhupen Hazarika's works are deeply rooted in the ethos of Assam and its people. His songs are known for their rich commentary on **social issues, human struggles, and the cultural legacy of Assam**.
 
• He is also credited with introducing Assamese and North-East Indian folk music and culture to a wider Indian and global audience, making him an integral figure in India's cultural landscape.
 
• Through his artistic contributions, he earned the title “Bard,” which denotes a poet and storyteller, highlighting his unique ability to narrate the stories of the Brahmaputra River and the Assamese people through his music and lyrics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dr. Bhupen Hazarika’s Early Life:**

 
 
• He was born on **8 September 1926** in Sadiya, Assam.
 
• Dr. Hazarika showed an early inclination towards music and performed his first song at the age of 10 in the Assamese language.
 
 
 
• **Significant Contributions:**
 
 
• Dr. Hazarika's songs often revolved around the themes of **humanity, communal harmony, and social justice**. He used his music as a tool to bring attention to the struggles of the common people, particularly in Assam.
 
• He wrote and composed music for numerous films in Assamese, Bengali, and Hindi, contributing significantly to Indian cinema and culture.
 
• His most notable works include songs such as **"Bistirno Parore,"** which is inspired by the Brahmaputra River, and **"Manuhe Manuhar Babe,"** a song of universal brotherhood.
 
 
 
• **Awards and Honors:**
 
 
• Dr. Bhupen Hazarika received numerous awards, including the **Padma Bhushan (2001)**, the **Dadasaheb Phalke Award (1992)**, and the **Bharat Ratna (2019, posthumously)**, India's highest civilian award.
 
• He was also awarded the **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award** and honored at several international festivals for his contributions to music and culture.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Dr. Hazarika's music continues to inspire millions and remains a symbol of Assamese pride and culture.
 
• The **Brahmaputra River** has become synonymous with his name, as his songs immortalized its beauty and role in the lives of Assamese people.
 
• The **Dr. Bhupen Hazarika Setu (Dhola-Sadiya Bridge)**, the longest bridge in India, was named in his honor, solidifying his legacy in Assam and India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Titles for Dr. Bhupen Hazarika:**

 
 
• While “Bard of Brahmaputra” is his most famous title, he was also referred to as the **Voice of Assam** due to his significant role in promoting Assamese music and culture.
 
 
 
• **Brahmaputra River:**
 
 
• The **Brahmaputra River**, one of the major rivers in India, flows through Assam and is a lifeline for the people of the region. Dr. Hazarika’s works often depicted its cultural and economic importance.
 
 
 
• **Contribution to Indian Cinema:**
 
 
• Dr. Hazarika worked as a director, music composer, and lyricist in several Assamese, Bengali, and Hindi films, blending folk music with modern elements.

question: Who was awarded the 2025 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for a novel that serves as a provocative and satirical reimagining of the life of Jim from Mark Twain’s 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Percival Everett**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Percival Everett** is a celebrated American author known for his works of literary fiction that often explore themes of race, identity, and societal norms.
 
• The novel awarded the **2025 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction** is a provocative and satirical reimagining of the life of Jim, a significant character from Mark Twain’s **'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'**.
 
• Jim’s portrayal in Twain’s work is complex, and Everett’s novel provides a contemporary lens to explore his life, addressing themes of racial injustice and societal stereotypes.
 
• The Pulitzer Prize is one of the most prestigious literary awards, recognizing works of excellence in journalism, literature, and musical composition in the United States.
 
• Everett’s novel was acclaimed for its bold storytelling, unique perspective, and its ability to challenge readers to rethink historical narratives and cultural perceptions.

• **The Pulitzer Prize:**
 
 
• The Pulitzer Prize was established in **1917** by provisions in the will of Joseph Pulitzer, a newspaper publisher.
 
• It awards excellence in **21 categories**, including fiction, drama, poetry, and journalism.
 
• The Fiction category honors distinguished works by American authors, dealing primarily with American life.
 
• Winning this prize is considered one of the highest accolades in the field of literature.
 
 
 
• **'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn' by Mark Twain:**
 
 
• Published in **1884**, this novel is regarded as one of the greatest American works of literature.
 
• The character Jim, a runaway slave, plays a central role in the story and serves as a lens to examine themes like freedom, morality, and racism.
 
• Twain’s portrayal of Jim has been both praised and critiqued for its complexity and representation of African Americans during the 19th century.
 
 
 
• **Reimagining Historical Narratives:**
 
 
• Authors like Percival Everett use historical fiction to reinterpret iconic characters and events, often addressing societal issues through a modern lens.
 
• Reimagining Jim’s life offers an opportunity to discuss systemic racism, stereotypes, and the legacy of slavery in America.
 
• This approach bridges the gap between classical literature and contemporary social discourse.

question:
Following statements are made regarding global warming.

A. Global warming is the long-term heating of Earth's surface observed since the preindustrial period due to human activities, primarily fossil fuel burning, which increases heat-trapping greenhouse gas levels in Earth's atmosphere.

B. Global warming causes climate change, which poses a serious threat to life on Earth in the forms of widespread flooding and extreme weather.

Which of these statements are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A & B**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Global warming** 

 
 
• Global warming refers to the long-term trend of rising temperatures on **Earth's surface**, which has been observed since the preindustrial period.
 
• The Earth's temperature is regulated by a balance between incoming solar radiation and outgoing radiation reflected back into space.
 
• **Greenhouse gases**, such as **carbon dioxide**, **methane**, and **nitrous oxide**,** trap **some of the outgoing radiation, which keeps the Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
 
• The Industrial Revolution, which began in the mid-18th century, marked the start of significant **human-caused emissions of greenhouse gases**.
 
• Since then, the use of fossil fuels for energy, transportation, and industrial purposes has grown rapidly, leading to an **unprecedented increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide** levels.
 
• Multiple lines of evidence, including temperature records, **ice core data**, and **ocean temperature** measurements, all support the conclusion that the Earth is warming due to human activities.
 
• The consequences of global warming are** vast** and** potentially catastrophic**.
 
• Rising temperatures can lead to more frequent and severe heatwaves, droughts, wildfires, and storms, threatening human lives and causing significant economic damage.
 
• Global warming also contributes to sea-level rise, ocean acidification, and the loss of biodiversity, further exacerbating the environmental impact.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/cd5c44b5cf473234011f68ec41886c08c55ca3faf9b62e29e211de08b831c1dd.png] 

**Note** - Global warming and the Greenhouse effect both are different things.

question: Which endemic species of owl of Central India is listed as Endangered in the IUCN Red List since 2018?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Forest Owlet**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Forest Owlet (*Heteroglaux blewitti*) is an endemic species to Central India.
 
• It has been listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2018.
 
• This species was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1997.
 
• The Forest Owlet is primarily found in the forests of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.
 
• Its population is estimated to be fewer than 250 mature individuals, making it critically endangered.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **IUCN Red List:**

 
 
• The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List is a critical indicator of the health of the world’s biodiversity.
 
• It provides information about the global extinction risk status of animal, fungus, and plant species.
 
• Species are categorized into nine groups: Not Evaluated, Data Deficient, Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, and Extinct.
 
 
 
• **Endangered Species:**
 
 
• Endangered species are those at a very high risk of extinction in the wild.
 
• Factors contributing to the endangered status include habitat loss, poaching, and climate change.
 
• Conservation efforts are crucial to prevent their extinction.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Efforts:**
 
 
• Conservation efforts for endangered species like the Forest Owlet include habitat protection, anti-poaching measures, and breeding programs.
 
• Organizations like the Wildlife Conservation Society and BirdLife International are actively involved in such efforts.
 
 
 
• **Habitat of Forest Owlet:**
 
 
• The Forest Owlet prefers deciduous forests with dense undergrowth.
 
• Conservation of these habitats is crucial for its survival.

question: Which international treaty was adopted in 1992 to combat global warming and prepare for its effects?

options.text: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer
Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

solution:
The correct answer is __**United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was adopted in 1992 at the Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
 
• The primary objective of the UNFCCC is to stabilize greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere to prevent dangerous human interference with the climate system.
 
• It serves as the foundation for global efforts to combat climate change and has been ratified by 197 parties, including nearly all countries worldwide.
 
• The UNFCCC led to the establishment of the annual Conference of the Parties (COP), where nations meet to negotiate and review progress in addressing climate change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kyoto Protocol:**

 
 
• A landmark international treaty adopted under the UNFCCC in 1997 and came into force in 2005.
 
• It legally binds developed countries to emission reduction targets.
 
• It introduced market-based mechanisms like emissions trading, clean development mechanism (CDM), and joint implementation (JI).
 
 
 
• **Paris Agreement:**
 
 
• An agreement within the UNFCCC adopted in 2015 and came into force in 2016.
 
• It aims to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, preferably to 1.5 degrees Celsius, compared to pre-industrial levels.
 
• Countries submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) outlining their climate actions.
 
 
 
• **Green Climate Fund (GCF):**
 
 
• Established under the UNFCCC in 2010 to assist developing countries in adaptation and mitigation practices to counter climate change.
 
• Aims to mobilize $100 billion per year by 2020 from various sources.
 
 
 
• **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC):**
 
 
• Provides scientific assessments on climate change to inform policy decisions.
 
• Established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).

question:
Regarding the legal protection of Dugong (Sea Cow) in India, consider the following statements:**
Statement 1:** The Dugong is protected under **Schedule I** of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.**
Statement 2:** This classification provides the Dugong with the highest level of legal protection, similar to that of the Tiger.**
Which of the statements given above is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Both Statement 1 and Statement 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** The Dugong (Sea Cow) is protected under **Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**, which ensures the highest level of legal protection for species in India. *Hence, Statement 1 is correct.*
 
• **Statement 2:** Being included under Schedule I means Dugong receives the same level of protection as the **Tiger**, as both are considered critically important for conservation. *Hence, Statement 2 is correct.*
 
• The Dugong is a marine herbivorous mammal, classified as **vulnerable** globally under the IUCN Red List. In India, its conservation is a priority due to its declining population.
 
• Legal protection under Schedule I prohibits activities like hunting, capturing, or harming Dugongs, and violators face stringent penalties under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
 
• The Dugong’s habitat, predominantly in shallow coastal waters like the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, further necessitates robust legal protection.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972:**

 
 
• It is a comprehensive law enacted to protect wildlife and their habitats in India.
 
• Species under **Schedule I** enjoy the **maximum protection**, with penalties for violations including fines and imprisonment.
 
• The Act also provides provisions for the establishment of protected areas like National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.
 
 
 
• **Dugong Conservation:**
 
 
• The Dugong’s population in India is threatened by habitat loss, hunting, and accidental entanglement in fishing nets.
 
• Several conservation initiatives like the **Dugong Recovery Program** have been launched to protect its population and habitat.
 
• Dugongs are primarily found in the **Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park**, which is a critical conservation site.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Tiger Conservation:**
 
 
• Both Dugong and Tiger are listed under Schedule I, ensuring the highest level of protection.
 
• Tiger conservation has seen success through programs like **Project Tiger**, which serves as a model for Dugong conservation strategies.
 
• The focus on habitat restoration and community involvement is crucial for both species.
 
 
 
• **Threats to Dugongs:**
 
 
• Destruction of seagrass beds, which are the primary food source for Dugongs.
 
• Pollution and sedimentation affecting coastal ecosystems.
 
• Illegal hunting and fishing practices.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Status:** Dugongs are classified as **Vulnerable** on the IUCN Red List and are protected under Appendix I of CITES.
 
• **Habitat:** Dugongs inhabit shallow waters of tropical and subtropical regions, relying heavily on **seagrass meadows**.
 
• **Government Initiatives:** India has implemented measures like **habitat restoration**, awareness campaigns, and collaboration with local communities to protect Dugongs.
 
• **International Conservation:** The Dugong is a focus of international conservation efforts, including the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS).

question: Which artificial element has been provisionally named seaborgium by American researchers in honour of Nobel Laureate Glenn T Seaborg?
solution:
Correct Answer **Element 106**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **artificial element** that has been provisionally named **seaborgium** in honor of **Nobel Laureate Glenn T. Seaborg** is the chemical element with **atomic number 106.**
 
• It is a synthetic element, meaning that it does not occur naturally on Earth and can only be produced artificially through **nuclear reactions.**
 
• The discovery of seaborgium was announced in **1974** by a team of **American researchers** at the **Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory** in **California**.
 
• It was named in honor of **Glenn T. Seaborg,** who was a pioneer in the field of nuclear chemistry and played a key role in the discovery of several other synthetic elements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information:__**

 
• In 1869, Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev created the framework that became the modern periodic table
 
• He also left gaps for elements that were yet to be discovered.
 
• While arranging the elements according to their atomic weight, if he found that they did not fit into the group he would rearrange them.
 
• British chemist John Newlands was the first to arrange the elements into a periodic table with increasing order of atomic masses.
 
• He arranged the elements in eight groups but left no gaps for undiscovered elements.
 
• Gregor Mendel, through his work on pea plants, discovered the fundamental laws of inheritance.
 
• Mendel tracked the segregation of parental genes and their appearance in the offspring as dominant or recessive traits.
 
• In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a theory for the hydrogen atom, based on the quantum theory that some physical quantities only take discrete values.
 
• Dalton's atomic theory suggested that all matter was comprised of indivisible and indestructible atoms with distinct masses and properties, the combination of which determined the physical nature of their constituent elements.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT with respect to Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, proposed in 2022?

A. Online games will have to register with a self-regulatory body, and only games cleared by the body will be allowed to legally operate in India.

B. Online gaming companies will not be allowed to engage in betting on the outcome of games, the proposed rules say.

C. According to the rules, there could be more than one self-regulatory body.
solution:
Correct Answer **A, B and C**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY) **has **released the draft rules **pertaining to **online gaming **by amending the **Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. **
 
• These rules are **released by MEITY** for the comments of the public and shall remain open for such comments till **17th Jan. 2023.**
 
• he proposed rules add definitions for **online games and online gaming intermediaries** and put restrictions on games related to **betting, gambling, or the participation of minors.**
 
• **Online gaming **intermediaries will need to register with a **self-regulatory body,** which must be registered with the **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology**, and must display their registration details on their website or mobile application.
 
• The **self-regulatory body **will be composed of several individuals with different backgrounds, and the online gaming intermediary must display a visible mark of registration on all online games registered by the **self-regulatory body.**
 
• Gaming companies will also have to secure a Random Number Generation Certificate to ensure game outputs are statistically random and unpredictable, and a **"no bot certificate" **from a reputed certifying body.
 
• Online intermediaries will be required to identify and verify the identity of the user **(KYC**) while starting a user account-based relationship.
 
• They will also need to appoint a **Chief Compliance Officer,** a nodal contact person, and publish a physical contact address in India on their website or mobile application.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** Why in the news?

 
• Social media platforms and other intermediaries on the Internet are now required to remove PIB-flagged fake news articles about the Union Government from their platforms.
 
• The new amendment of the IT Rules means that Social media platforms will no longer enjoy legal immunity on content posted by their users.
 
 
• Platforms can now be called as a party in court proceedings. *Hence statement 1 is correct*.
 
• Minister of State for Electronics and Information Technology said that platforms will not be required to take down content due to this Rule alone, but they will not enjoy the legal immunity that they currently benefit from for content posted by their users. They can now be called as a party in court proceedings.
 
 
 
• The changes were notified through the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2023, amending the IT Rules, 2021.

Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2023:

 
• Social Media Platforms:

 
 
• The rules require social media platforms with a certain number of users in the country to establish a physical presence, including a registered office, in the country.
 
• This aims to ensure that these platforms are more accountable to the laws and regulations of the country and can be held liable for any content that violates the rules.
 
 
 
• Content Removal and Traceability:
 
 
• The rules mandate social media platforms to remove or disable access to any unlawful content or information.a
 
• They are also required to maintain records of the origin of information, which can be used to trace the originator of any unlawful content.
 
• This is aimed at combating the spread of fake news, misinformation, and illegal content online.
 
 
 
• User verification:
 
 
• Social media intermediaries are required to take measures to verify the identity of their users, especially for significant social media intermediaries.
 
 
 
• Voluntary user verification:
 
 
• The IT Rules now allow for voluntary user verification, which means users have the option to verify their accounts with social media intermediaries using government-issued ID proofs.
 
 
 
• Emergency blocking of content:
 
 
• In cases where there is an emergency situation that threatens public order, the government can direct social media intermediaries to block access to certain content within 24 hours.
 
 
 
• Data retention:
 
 
• Social media intermediaries are required to retain user data for 180 days for investigation and prevention of cybersecurity incidents, and they are also required to provide information to the government agencies as and when requested.
 
 
 
• Grievance Redressal Mechanism:
 
 
• Social media platforms are required to establish a grievance redressal mechanism to address complaints from users and resolve them in a timely manner.
 
• This aims to provide users with a channel to report objectionable content and seek remedies for any violations of their rights.
 
 
 
• Code of Ethics for Digital Media:
 
 
• The rules introduce a code of ethics for digital media, including online news portals and OTT (Over-The-Top) platforms.
 
• This code includes guidelines related to the portrayal of prohibited content, journalistic conduct, and user-generated content.
 
• Digital media platforms are required to classify their content into appropriate categories and follow the prescribed code of ethics.
 
 
 
• Self-Regulatory Body:
 
 
• The rules provide for the establishment of a self-regulatory body by digital media platforms, which will oversee the implementation of the code of ethics and address grievances related to digital media. *Hence statement 2 is correct*.
 
• This self-regulatory body will be required to register with the government and comply with certain guidelines.
 
 
 
• Government Oversight:
 
 
• The rules also give the government the authority to issue directions to social media platforms and digital media platforms for compliance with the rules.
 
• Failure to comply with these directions can result in penalties and other legal consequences.

question:
Read the below statements:**
1. NASA launched a space telescope, SPHEREx, to study the universe's "cosmic glow".

2. The Major Atmospheric Cherenkov Experiment (MACE) telescope was inaugurated at Hanle, Ladakh.

Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Statement 1 and Statement 2 both**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **NASA launched the SPHEREx space telescope:**

 
 
• **SPHEREx** (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer) is a space telescope developed by **NASA**.
 
• Its primary goal is to study the universe’s "cosmic glow," also known as the **background infrared radiation**.
 
• The mission will help scientists understand the formation and evolution of galaxies, the distribution of water and organic molecules in space, and the history of the universe.
 
• SPHEREx will map the sky in **96 different color bands** to capture a detailed view of the cosmos. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*
 
 
 
• **MACE telescope inaugurated at Hanle, Ladakh:**
 
 
• The **Major Atmospheric Cherenkov Experiment (MACE) telescope** is one of the largest gamma-ray telescopes in the world.
 
• It was installed at **Hanle, Ladakh**, which is home to India’s high-altitude astronomical observatory.
 
• The telescope is designed to detect Cherenkov radiation, which occurs when high-energy gamma rays interact with the Earth’s atmosphere.
 
• This facility strengthens India’s position in the field of **gamma-ray astronomy** and contributes to the study of **cosmic phenomena** such as pulsars, supernovae, and black holes. *Hence, statement 2 is correct.*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **SPHEREx Mission:**

 
 
• **Full Form:** Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer.
 
• **Launch Year:** Planned for **2025**.
 
• It will survey the entire sky four times, collecting data from over **300 million galaxies** and **100 million stars** in the Milky Way.
 
• SPHEREx will help identify the building blocks of life by studying the distribution of **water and organic molecules** in the interstellar medium.
 
• **Cosmic Infrared Background:** The mission aims to decode the history of star formation and galaxy evolution through infrared observations.
 
 
 
• **MACE Telescope:**
 
 
• **Location:** Hanle, Ladakh, India.
 
• **Primary Function:** Detects Cherenkov radiation to study high-energy cosmic gamma rays.
 
• **Operational Altitude:** Situated at an altitude of approximately **4,300 meters** above sea level.
 
• **Significance:** Supports research in **astrophysics**, including studies on **gamma-ray bursts, supernova remnants, and active galactic nuclei**.
 
• **Global Importance:** It is one of the largest telescopes of its kind, enhancing international collaboration in gamma-ray astronomy.
 
 
 
• **Gamma-ray Astronomy:**
 
 
• **Purpose:** Focuses on studying celestial phenomena emitting gamma rays, the highest-energy form of electromagnetic radiation.
 
• **Applications:** Helps explore black holes, neutron stars, and the origins of cosmic rays.
 
• **Detection Technique:** Cherenkov telescopes detect gamma-ray interactions with the Earth’s atmosphere through light flashes called Cherenkov radiation.
 
• **Global Facilities:** Other major gamma-ray observatories include the **High Energy Stereoscopic System (HESS)** in Namibia and the **VERITAS** observatory in the USA.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hanle Observatory:**

 
 
• Operated by the **Indian Institute of Astrophysics** (IIA).
 
• Home to other key facilities like the **Indian Astronomical Observatory** and the Himalayan Chandra Telescope.
 
• Known for its **clear skies**, making it an ideal location for high-altitude astronomy.
 
 
 
• **NASA Space Missions:**
 
 
• **James Webb Space Telescope (JWST):** Focuses on infrared astronomy and studying the formation of stars and galaxies.
 
• **Hubble Space Telescope:** An iconic telescope known for its contributions to understanding the universe’s expansion and distant galaxies.
 
• **Chandra X-ray Observatory:** Specializes in studying high-energy phenomena like black holes and supernovae.
 
• SPHEREx continues NASA’s legacy of pioneering space observatories for understanding cosmic evolution.

question: Which of the following **correctly** describes the NISAR mission?

options.text: Optical imaging mission for exoplanet detection
ISRO-only mission for X-band radar mapping
Joint ISRO–NASA mission using L and S-band radar

solution:
The correct answer is __**Joint ISRO–NASA mission using L and S-band radar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **NISAR Mission** is a collaborative project between **NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration)** and **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)**. It is designed to provide global, all-weather, high-resolution radar imaging of Earth.
 
• The mission will use dual-frequency radar systems, specifically **L-band and S-band radar**, to generate accurate and detailed images of the Earth's surface.
 
• The **L-band radar** is being developed by NASA, while the **S-band radar** is being developed by ISRO. Together, they will provide a unique capability to measure changes in Earth's land surface, ice sheets, and ecosystems.
 
• The satellite is expected to monitor a wide range of phenomena, including **land subsidence, deforestation, glacier movements, earthquakes, and agricultural patterns**.
 
• The **launch** of the NISAR satellite is planned to take place from India on an ISRO-built **GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle)**.

question: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is caused by duplication of the peripheral myelin protein-22 (PMP22) gene on which chromosome?
solution:
The correct answer is __**chromosome 17**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT)** is one of the most common inherited neurological disorders, affecting the peripheral nerves.
 
• It is specifically caused by the **duplication of the PMP22 gene** located on chromosome 17.
 
• The disease leads to the progressive loss of muscle tissue and touch sensation, primarily in the feet, legs, hands, and arms.
 
• CMT can be classified into several types, with CMT1A being the most common form linked to the duplication of PMP22.
 
• Diagnosis often involves genetic testing to identify the duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **PMP22 Gene:**

 
 
• The Peripheral Myelin Protein 22 (PMP22) gene plays a crucial role in the structure and function of myelin, the protective sheath around nerves.
 
• Overexpression of PMP22 due to gene duplication disrupts the production of normal myelin, leading to nerve degeneration.
 
 
 
• **Symptoms of CMT:**
 
 
• Common symptoms include muscle weakness, decreased muscle size, decreased sensation in extremities, foot deformities, and difficulty walking.
 
• Symptoms typically appear in adolescence or early adulthood.
 
 
 
• **Types of CMT:**
 
 
• CMT1: Caused by abnormalities in myelin.
 
• CMT2: Caused by abnormalities in the axon of the peripheral nerve cell.
 
• CMTX: X-linked inheritance pattern, often affecting males more severely.
 
 
 
• **Treatment and Management:**
 
 
• There is currently no cure for CMT; treatment focuses on managing symptoms.

question: In which year did Walter Fleming stain the chromosomes to see them clearly and describe the entire process of mitosis?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1882**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Walter Fleming, a German biologist, is renowned for his pioneering work in cell division.
 
• In 1882, he developed a technique to stain chromosomes, allowing them to be seen more clearly under a microscope.
 
• Fleming meticulously described the entire process of mitosis, coining the term "mitosis" to describe this type of cell division.
 
• His work laid the foundation for understanding the mechanisms of cell division and the behavior of chromosomes during this process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chromosomes:** Thread-like structures located within the nucleus of animal and plant cells that contain DNA.
 
• **Mitosis:** A type of cell division that results in two daughter cells each having the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
 
• **Staining Techniques:** Methods used to enhance the contrast in samples, generally at the microscopic level, by using dyes.
 
• **Cell Division:** The process by which a parent cell divides into two or more daughter cells, crucial for growth and development in living organisms.
 
• **Histology:** The study of the microscopic structure of tissues, which was significantly advanced by Fleming's staining techniques.

question: What do you call the drugs that bind to the receptor site and inhibit its natural function?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Antagonists**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Antagonists**

 
 
• **Drugs that bind to the receptor site and inhibit its natural function are called Antagonists.**
 
• Antagonists and agonists act differently.
 
• Agonists combine with the receptor molecule and produce a biological response but antagonists combine with the receptors and inhibit their natural function.
 
• Enzyme inhibitors inhibit the catalytic activity of the enzyme. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Antidepressants**

 
 
• Antidepressants are **medications** prescribed to treat various forms of **depression **and** anxiety disorders**.
 
• They work by affecting neurotransmitters in the brain, such as **serotonin, norepinephrine, **and **dopamine**, which play a role in mood regulation. 
 
 
 
• **Agonist**
 
 
• An agonist is a molecule or compound that activates a receptor, leading to a physiological or pharmacological response in a **cell or organism**.
 
• Agonists can be naturally occurring, like **hormones** or **neurotransmitters**, or** synthetic**, like **drugs**. 
 
 
 
• **Depressants**
 
 
• Depressants are substances that slow down the **central nervous system** (CNS),** reducing neural activity **and** leading to relaxation**,** drowsiness**, and **decreased alertness**.
 
• They can have therapeutic uses, such as treating **anxiety**,** insomnia**, and** muscle spasms**.
 
• Common depressants include alcohol, benzodiazepines (e.g., **Valium, Xanax**), barbiturates, and certain sleep medications.

question: In which year was the fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicolson? The model commonly represented cell membrane structure and dynamics.
solution:
The correct answer is __**1972**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The fluid mosaic model was proposed by S.J. Singer and G.L. Nicolson in **1972**.
 
• This model describes the structure of cell membranes as a mosaic of components that gives the membrane a fluid character.
 
• It emphasizes that the cell membrane is flexible and constantly in motion, rather than being static.
 
• The model was revolutionary for illustrating the dynamic nature of the lipid bilayer and the embedded proteins.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lipid Bilayer:**

 
 
• A double layer of lipids that forms the core structure of the cell membrane.
 
• Each lipid molecule has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) head and two hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails.
 
 
 
• **Integral Proteins:**
 
 
• Proteins that are embedded within the lipid bilayer.
 
• They can span the entire membrane (transmembrane proteins) or be attached to only one side.
 
 
 
• **Peripheral Proteins:**
 
 
• Proteins that are attached to the exterior or interior surfaces of the lipid bilayer.
 
• They are not embedded within the lipid bilayer.
 
 
 
• **Fluidity:**
 
 
• Refers to the viscous nature of the lipid bilayer, allowing lateral movement of molecules within the layer.
 
• Fluidity is influenced by temperature and the composition of the lipid molecules.
 
 
 
• **Mosaic Nature:**
 
 
• Describes the heterogeneous composition of the cell membrane, including lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates.
 
• These components are not uniformly distributed, contributing to the diverse functionality of the cell membrane.

Correct Answer** Iron**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** __Explanation:__

__
 
• Haemoglobin is a protein in your red blood cells that carries oxygen to your body's organs and tissues and transports carbon dioxide from your organs and tissues back to your lungs.
 
• Haemoglobin is essential for transferring oxygen in your blood from the lungs to the tissues.
 
• About 70 percent of your body's iron is found in the red blood cells of your blood called haemoglobin and in muscle cells called myoglobin.
 
• Iron is the essential element of Hemoglobin.__
 
• Iron-deficient anaemia is a type of anaemia.
 
• Red blood cells carry a biomolecule known as Hemoglobin.
 
• The haemoglobin is responsible for binding oxygen molecule to itself and carrying it around the various human organs through the bloodstream.
 
• Iron is the central atom in the biomolecule haemoglobin. The low concentration of iron affects the function of the bloodstream significantly to assure the availability of oxygen.
 
• Therefore, anaemic patients are deficient in iron.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/a12dd00de7ce21d3e840a77cba86773f3d612a89a389a4a7527c02d348fe6e51.png] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points:__**

 
• If a haemoglobin test reveals that your haemoglobin level is lower than normal, it means you have a low red blood cell count (Anemia). 
 
• Haemoglobin electrophoresis measures haemoglobin levels and looks for abnormal types of haemoglobin.
 
• It's most often used to help diagnose anaemia, sickle cell disease, and other haemoglobin disorders.
 
• The normal range for haemoglobin is: For men, 13.5 to 17.5 grams per deciliter. For women, 12.0 to 15.5 grams per deciliter.
 
• Haemoglobin is produced in bone marrow by erythrocytes and is circulated with them until their destruction.
 
• It is then broken down in the spleen, and some of its components, such as iron, are recycled to the bone marrow.

options.text: planning and prioritising nutrition intervention(s) to meet nutritional needs

solution:
The correct answer is __assessing psychological stress__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Assessing psychological stress is an important aspect of overall health and well-being, and it can certainly impact a person's nutritional status and food choices.
 
• However, it may not be considered a part of nutritional care during illness for several reasons.
 
• Firstly, nutritional care during illness typically focuses on the specific nutritional needs and challenges that arise as a result of the illness itself.
 
 
• This includes assessing the impact of the illness on a person's appetite, digestion, and nutrient requirements, as well as identifying any barriers to meeting those needs.
 
 
 
• Secondly, while psychological stress can certainly impact a person's nutritional status, it may be better addressed through other means.
 
 
• For example, a person experiencing significant stress or anxiety may benefit from counselling, stress reduction techniques, or other forms of mental health support.
 
 
 
• Lastly, in some cases, addressing nutritional needs may actually help alleviate some of the symptoms of psychological stress.
 
 
• For example, certain nutrients, such as omega-3 fatty acids and B vitamins, have been shown to have a positive impact on mood and cognitive function.
 
 
 
• Overall, while assessing psychological stress may not be considered a part of nutritional care during illness, it is certainly an important aspect of overall health and well-being that should be addressed as needed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The food components gradually get digested as food travels through the various compartments.
 
• The inner walls of the stomach and the small intestine, and the various glands associated with the canal such as salivary glands, the liver and the pancreas secrete digestive juices.
 
• The digestive juices convert complex substances of food into simpler ones.
 
• The digestive tract and the associated glands together constitute the digestive system.

question: Among the following diseases, which one is NOT inherited?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Down syndrome**, **Cystic fibrosis**, and **Muscular dystrophy** are genetic disorders passed from parents to children through genes.
 
• **Malaria** is caused by the Plasmodium parasites, which are transmitted to people through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

• Understanding the difference between genetic and infectious diseases is crucial for diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies.

 Disease Type
 Description

 Conditions caused by abnormalities in genes or chromosomes. Some may be inherited, while others occur due to mutations or changes in genes.

 Diseases caused by pathogenic microorganisms, such as bacteria, viruses, parasites, or fungi; can be spread, directly or indirectly, from one person to another.

 An infectious disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes.

question: Which amino acid is a precursor to serotonin, a neurotransmitter that regulates your appetite, sleep and mood?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Tryptophan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tryptophan** is an essential amino acid that serves as a precursor for serotonin synthesis in the human body.
 
• Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that plays a critical role in regulating mood, appetite, and sleep.
 
• Tryptophan is absorbed from dietary sources such as turkey, chicken, milk, cheese, yogurt, eggs, nuts, seeds, tofu, and soy products.
 
• Once ingested, tryptophan undergoes hydroxylation and decarboxylation to produce serotonin in the brain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Serotonin**

 
 
• Serotonin is also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT).
 
• It is primarily found in the gastrointestinal tract, blood platelets, and the central nervous system.
 
• In the brain, serotonin is involved in the regulation of mood, anxiety, and happiness.
 
• Abnormal levels of serotonin are linked to depression, anxiety disorders, and other mood disorders.
 
 
 
• **Essential Amino Acids**
 
 
• Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
 
• There are nine essential amino acids, including tryptophan, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, and valine.
 
 
 
• **Hydroxylation and Decarboxylation**
 
 
• Hydroxylation is a chemical process that introduces a hydroxyl group (-OH) into an organic compound.
 
• Decarboxylation is a chemical reaction that removes a carboxyl group and releases carbon dioxide (CO₂).
 
 
 
• **Dietary Sources of Tryptophan**
 
 
• Animal-based sources: Turkey, chicken, milk, cheese, yogurt, and eggs.
 
• Plant-based sources: Nuts, seeds, tofu, soy products, and legumes.

question: Which of the following can degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances?
solution:
The correct answer is **Fungal enzymes**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**

__
 
• Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.
 
• The word catabolism is from New Latin, which got the roots from Greek: κάτω Kato, "downward" and βάλλειν ballein, "to throw".
 
• It breaks down large molecules like polysaccharides, lipids, etc. into smaller units like monosaccharides, fatty acids, nucleotides, etc.
 
• It is the breaking-down aspect of metabolism.
 
• Cells use the monomers released from breaking down polymers to either construct new polymer molecules or degrade them into simple waste products like lactic acid, carbon dioxide, acetic acid, urea, and ammonia, releasing energy.
 
• The creation of these wastes is usually an oxidation process involving a release of chemical-free energy. Of this, some are lost as heat, and the rest results in the formation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information:__**

 
• Catabolism is a metabolic process in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones with the release of energy. In the context of the given statement, bacterial and fungal enzymes break down the complex detritus into simpler inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water, and mineral ions. This breakdown process releases energy that can be used by the decomposers or other organisms in the ecosystem.
 
• Fragmentation: Detritivores (e.g., earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation.
 
• Leaching: By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
 
• Decomposition: It is the process of breaking down a substance into its constituent parts. Decomposition of dead organic matter occurs in nature and it is also called decay or putrefaction.​

__
 
• Invertebrates with pentaradial symmetry, spiny skin, a water circulatory system, and a simple nervous system are known as echinoderms.
 
• There are around 7,000 extant species in this phylum.
 
• Echinodermata are only found in the sea.
 
• Echinoderms include sea stars, sea cucumbers, sea urchins, sand dollars, and brittle stars.
 
• Echinoderms feature a calcareous endoskeleton with pentaradial symmetry and pigment cells that give them a wide spectrum of hues, as well as cells that contain poisons.
 
• Water circulates through an echinoderm's water vascular system, which is made up of a central ring of canals that extends along each arm for gaseous exchange and nutrition.
 
• Echinoderms have two sexes that release their eggs and sperm into the water, where the sperm fertilizes the eggs.ও
 
• Echinoderms have the ability to reproduce asexually through regeneration.
 
• The neurological system of echinoderms is exceedingly simple, consisting of a nerve ring in the center and five radial nerves radiating outward along the arms; there is no brain.​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

• Phylum Annelida contains the class Polychaeta (the polychaetes) and the class Oligochaeta (the earthworms, leeches, and their relatives). 
 
• These species can be found in a variety of settings, including marine, terrestrial, and freshwater, but the presence of water or humidity is essential for their survival, especially in terrestrial habitats.
 
• This phylum's animals form parasitic and commensal symbioses with other species in their environment.
 
• Because of its important property of metamerism, or real segmentation, annelids are commonly referred to as "segmented worms" throughout embryonic stages.

• Arthropods have an open circulatory system and can breathe through their book gills, book lungs, or tracheal tubes.

• The digestive, nervous, excretory, reproductive, and respiratory systems are all part of the mollusk's visceral mass.
 
• Most mollusks have a radula, which looks like a tongue but has teeth-like projections for shredding or scraping food.

• Thallophytes are a polyphyletic class of immobile organisms that are put together based on shared traits but have no common ancestor.
 
• They used to be considered a member of the kingdom Plantae.

• Ferns, horsetails, and club mosses are a few examples.

• Neutrons play a crucial role in the stability of atomic nuclei.
 
 
 
• **Alpha particles:**
 
 
• Alpha particles are a type of ionizing radiation ejected by certain radioactive materials.
 
• They consist of two protons and two neutrons bound together.
 
• Alpha particles are relatively heavy and positively charged.
 
 
 
• **Nobel Prize in Physics:**
 
 
• It is one of the most prestigious awards in the field of physics.
 
• James Chadwick received this honor in 1935 for his discovery of the neutron.
 
• The Nobel Prize in Physics recognizes outstanding contributions to the field of physics.
 
 
 
• **Nuclear Physics:**
 
 
• It is a branch of physics that studies the constituents and interactions of atomic nuclei.
 
• The discovery of the neutron was a major milestone in nuclear physics.
 
• Nuclear physics has applications in various fields, including energy production and medical imaging.

__
 
• The Hydroxyl (-OH) functional group attached to the aliphatic carbon atom of the alkyl group forms alcohols.
 
• The general formula for alcohol is R-OH, where R is the alkyl group and -OH is the hydroxyl group.
 
• There are three types of alcohol: primary, secondary, and tertiary.
 
• Primary alcohols are those in which the carbon atom attached to the OH group is connected with one alkyl group (RCH2-OH).
 
• Secondary alcohols are those in which the carbon atom attached to the OH group is connected with two alkyl groups (R2CH-OH).
 
• Tertiary alcohols are those in which the carbon atom attached to the OH group is connected with three alkyl groups (R3C-OH).
 
• The general name for alcohol is 'alkyl alcohol', Ex: methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, etc.
 
• The IUPAC name of alcohols is written using the suffix 'ol' as an alkanol, Ex: methanol, ethanol, etc.

Aldehydes

 
• Aldehydes are the compound containing the -CHO (aldehyde) functional group.
 
• The general formula for aldehydes is R-CHO.

Ethers

__
 
• ** In 1845, the German chemist Hermann Kolbe published a method for the synthesis of acetic acid, which is a natural product containing two carbon atoms.**
 
• Kolbe's method involved the electrolysis of sodium acetate to produce** acetic acid and carbon dioxide.**
 
• This was a significant breakthrough in organic chemistry, as it demonstrated that organic compounds could be synthesized from **inorganic** starting materials using **chemical reactions.**
 
• Kolbe's work laid the foundation for the development of **modern organic chemistry** and helped to establish the concept of** structural isomerism.​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ** Friedrich Wohler (1800-1882) **was a **German chemist **who is best known for his synthesis of urea, which demonstrated that organic compounds could be artificially synthesized from inorganic starting materials.

 
 
• **In 1828, Wohler synthesized urea, **which is a naturally occurring organic compound found in urine, from inorganic materials, namely ammonium cyanate. 
 
 
 
• **Marcellin Berthelot (1827-1907) **was a **French chemist, politician, and historian of science**.
 
 
• He is best known for his work in thermochemistry, which is the study of the relationship between heat and chemical reactions.
 
• **Berthelot's contributions** to thermochemistry helped to establish the concept of energy conservation in chemical reactions and laid the foundation for the development of the field of physical chemistry.
 
 
 
• 
 
**Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac (1778-1850) was a French chemist and physicist who made important contributions to the fields of chemistry and gas laws.**

 
 
• 
 
He is best known for his work on the laws governing the behavior of gases, particularly his discovery of the law of combining volumes, which states that when gases combine chemically, they do so in volumes that are in a simple ratio to one another.

 
 
• 
 
**Gay-Lussac **also made significant contributions to the study of acids and bases, organic chemistry, and the chemical composition of water.

 
 
• 
 
He is credited with the discovery of cyanogen, a compound that contains both carbon and nitrogen, and he was the first to isolate boron and to suggest that it was an element.

question: What is the name of the ion with a charge of -1?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Anion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An ion with a charge of -1 is called an **anion**.
 
• Anions are formed when an atom gains one or more electrons, resulting in a net negative charge.
 
• Common examples of anions include chloride (Cl⁻), bromide (Br⁻), and iodide (I⁻).
 
• Anions play crucial roles in various chemical reactions and are essential in maintaining the charge balance in compounds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cation**

 
 
• A cation is an ion with a positive charge.
 
• Cations are formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
 
• Examples include sodium (Na⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), and potassium (K⁺).
 
 
 
• **Monovalent Ion**
 
 
• A monovalent ion has a charge of +1 or -1.
 
• Examples include hydrogen ion (H⁺) and fluoride ion (F⁻).
 
 
 
• **Polyvalent Ion**
 
 
• A polyvalent ion has a charge greater than +1 or -1.
 
• Examples include sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻).
 
 
 
• **Ions in Chemical Reactions**
 
 
• Ions are essential in the formation of ionic compounds.
 
• Ionic bonds are formed through the electrostatic attraction between cations and anions.
 
• Understanding ions is crucial for studying electrochemistry and various biological processes.

question: Which theory, independently introduced in 1923, led to the concept of acid base conjugate pairs?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Brønsted-Lowry theory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Brønsted-Lowry theory was independently introduced in 1923 by Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted and Thomas Martin Lowry.
 
• This theory defines acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
 
• It led to the concept of conjugate acid-base pairs, where an acid and a base differ by the presence or absence of a proton.
 
• Brønsted-Lowry theory expanded the definition of acids and bases beyond aqueous solutions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Arrhenius Theory:**

 
 
• Proposed by Svante Arrhenius in 1887.
 
• Defines acids as substances that increase the concentration of H₃O⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
 
• Bases are substances that increase the concentration of OH− ions in aqueous solution.
 
 
 
• **Lewis Theory:**
 
 
• Proposed by Gilbert N. Lewis in 1923.
 
• Defines acids as electron pair acceptors and bases as electron pair donors.
 
• Expands the concept of acids and bases to include reactions without protons.
 
 
 
• **Davy's Theory:**
 
 
• Proposed by Humphry Davy in the early 19th century.
 
• Suggested that acids contain replaceable hydrogen atoms.
 
• Davy's work helped to lay the groundwork for modern acid-base theories.
 
 
 
• **Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs:**
 
 
• In the Brønsted-Lowry theory, acids and bases form conjugate pairs.
 
• When an acid donates a proton, it forms its conjugate base.
 
• When a base accepts a proton, it forms its conjugate acid.

question: Which substance is commonly used as an acid-base indicator, which turns red in acidic solutions and blue in basic solutions?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Litmus paper**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Litmus paper** is a common acid-base indicator used in laboratories.
 
• It turns **red in acidic solutions** (pH less than 7).
 
• It turns **blue in basic solutions** (pH greater than 7).
 
• Litmus paper is derived from **lichens**, which are symbiotic associations between fungi and algae.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Substances that change color based on the pH level of the solution they are in.
 
• Common indicators include methyl orange, phenolphthalein, and bromothymol blue.
 
• Each indicator has a specific pH range over which it changes color.
 
 
 
• **pH Scale**
 
 
• A scale ranging from 0 to 14 used to measure how acidic or basic a solution is.
 
• A pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is basic.
 
 
 
• **Lichens**
 
 
• Organisms formed from a symbiotic relationship between fungi and algae.
 
• They are capable of surviving in harsh environments and are used to produce litmus.
 
 
 
• **Uses of Litmus Paper**
 
 
• Commonly used in educational laboratories to teach about acids and bases.
 
• Used for testing the acidity or alkalinity of various substances in industrial applications.
